title: A House Prepared, But for Whom?
scripture: Luke 11:15–26 Reflection | Making Room for God
theme: What if the peace we spend our lives searching for is found in something we have yet to recognize?
opening: Jesus describes a house swept clean and put in order, yet something terrible happens when its former occupant returns. What was missing from a house that appeared to have everything in its place?
prayer: Heavenly Father,    You created us in love and for love, yet so often we search for peace in things that cannot fully satisfy our hearts. Help us recognize Your presence, even when we do not understand the longing within us. When we fall, give us the humility to return to You. When we are tempted, strengthen us through Your grace. And when our hearts become distracted by the things of this world, remind us that our true home is with You.    May our hearts become a dwelling place for Your love, and may those who are still searching come to know the peace that only You can give.    Amen.
body:
In today's Gospel, Jesus has been driving out demons, yet some question the source of His authority. They accuse Him of acting through Beelzebul, the prince of demons.

Jesus responds with remarkable clarity. Why would Satan drive out Satan? A kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. Then He makes an extraordinary declaration:

“But if it is by the finger of God that I drive out demons, then the Kingdom of God has come upon you.”

The Kingdom of God is not simply something to anticipate. Through Jesus, it has already come among them. Yet some standing before Him cannot recognize what is happening before their very eyes.

Jesus continues with the image of a strong man guarding his possessions, only to be overcome by someone stronger. His armor is taken, and his spoils are distributed. The strong man represents Satan, and the stronger One is Christ. Jesus is revealing that He has come not merely to confront evil, but to overcome its power and liberate those held captive.

But He doesn't leave the lesson there.

Jesus describes an unclean spirit leaving a person and later returning to find its former home swept clean and put in order. The spirit then brings seven others more wicked than itself, leaving the person in a worse condition than before.

Why would Jesus describe a house that has been cleaned, only to become occupied again?

At first, we might wonder whether the house was ever truly clean. But Jesus tells us it was. The danger is not simply that evil may return, but that a life freed from evil must also become rooted in something greater.

And that brings us to the human heart.

We spend much of our lives searching for fulfillment. We seek love, security, accomplishments, possessions, and acceptance. These are not necessarily bad things. Many are beautiful gifts. Yet even when we have them, we may find ourselves searching for something more.

St. Augustine understood this longing when he wrote, “Our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

What if that longing has been with us from the beginning? What if, whether we recognize Him or not, we were created for a relationship with God?

Some discover this early in life. Others spend years searching, and some may never identify that longing as spiritual. There are also people who live generous, loving, and meaningful lives without professing belief in God. We cannot presume to know what is missing from another person's heart.

But we can ask ourselves whether the things we pursue can ever offer the lasting peace for which we were created.

Jesus' warning about the clean house begins to take on a deeper meaning. Removing what harms us is important, but what are we making room for?

A house can be swept clean and beautifully arranged, yet what makes it a home is the life and love within it.

Our hearts are no different.

And even those who love Christ deeply know that keeping our hearts turned toward Him is not always easy. Temptation is real. Human weakness is real. We fall, sometimes despite our sincere desire to remain faithful.

But falling does not mean our love was never genuine.

Christ knows our weakness. In His mercy, He has given us the Sacrament of Reconciliation, where we can bring our sins before Him and receive His forgiveness. We do not cleanse ourselves through our own strength. It is Christ who restores us through His grace.

What a gift, to know that when we have wandered, we can return.

And perhaps that is the distinction Jesus wants us to recognize. Our spiritual lives cannot be sustained merely by removing what is wrong. We must continue welcoming the One who makes us whole.

For those who already believe, this is a reminder to remain close to Him. For those who have drifted away, it is an invitation to return. And for those who have never known Him, it may simply be an invitation to consider the possibility that the peace we seek has a source greater than ourselves.

Jesus came as the stronger One, not simply to free us from evil, but to bring us into communion with God.

The question, then, is not whether we can keep our hearts perfectly clean through our own efforts.

It is whether we are making room for the One who desires to dwell within them.

A clean house is not meant to remain empty. It is a place where God is welcomed, where His love brings peace, and where our communion with Him can grow.

The table is set, and the invitation has been extended. There is a place for each of us at the feast in His Kingdom.

All are invited.
